concepts.title: RDS: Managed Relational Databases
concepts.description: RDS takes over patching, backups, and failover for a relational database engine you already know, but it draws its own version of the Shared Responsibility line -- understanding exactly what AWS takes over versus what you still fully own is what keeps a managed database from becoming a false sense of security.
learningObjectives: Explain what RDS actually automates compared to running the same database engine yourself on EC2, and what remains the customer's responsibility either way.
Explain how RDS Multi-AZ failover works and why it protects availability, not performance or scalability.
Distinguish a Multi-AZ standby from a read replica, including how each is used and what kind of failure or load each one addresses.
Explain automated backups and point-in-time recovery, including their actual recovery granularity and retention limits.
Diagnose a scenario where an application's read load is the bottleneck versus one where availability is the bottleneck, and choose the correct RDS feature for each.

sections.heading: What RDS Actually Takes Over
sections.body:
Amazon RDS runs a real relational database engine -- PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, or AWS's own Aurora -- but instead of you installing and operating that engine on an EC2 instance yourself, AWS provisions and manages the underlying compute and storage on your behalf. Concretely, RDS takes over the operating system entirely (you never see or patch a guest OS at all -- there's no SSH access to an RDS instance, full stop), applies engine patches and minor version upgrades on a schedule you configure, automates backups and storage scaling, and handles the mechanics of failover for a Multi-AZ deployment (covered in depth below).

This is a direct, concrete instance of the Shared Responsibility Model shifting further in the customer's favor, exactly as discussed when that model was first introduced earlier in this subject: with a self-managed database on EC2, you own OS patching, engine installation and patching, backup automation, and failover orchestration, on top of everything you'd own with RDS. What RDS does *not* take over, and what remains squarely yours regardless of how much of the operational burden it absorbs: your schema design, your query performance and indexing choices, your IAM and database-credential access control, your data's correctness, and critically, your instance sizing and Multi-AZ/read-replica configuration choices -- RDS automates the *mechanics* of the features you turn on, but it does not decide for you whether you need them, or size the instance correctly for your actual load. A poorly indexed query is exactly as slow on RDS as it would be on a self-managed database on EC2; RDS did not, and cannot, fix that.

sections.heading: Multi-AZ: Automated Failover, Not a Performance Feature
sections.body:
An RDS Multi-AZ deployment maintains a synchronously replicated standby copy of your database in a *different* Availability Zone from the primary -- the same AZ-diversification principle covered in the very first concept of this subject, applied specifically to a managed database. Every write to the primary is synchronously replicated to the standby before being acknowledged as durable, which means the standby is always caught up to the primary (at the cost of some added write latency, since the primary has to wait for that synchronous replication to complete). If the primary instance or its entire AZ fails, RDS automatically detects the failure and promotes the standby to become the new primary, typically completing the failover within roughly 60-120 seconds, and updates the database's DNS endpoint to point at the newly promoted instance -- your application doesn't need to be reconfigured with a new connection string, but it does need to handle a brief connection interruption during the failover window gracefully (typically via connection retry logic, which is worth building in explicitly rather than assuming failover is instantaneous and invisible).

The detail worth being precise about: **Multi-AZ exists purely for availability, not for performance or read scalability**. The standby instance is not available to serve any read traffic at all during normal operation -- it exists solely as a failover target, sitting idle from an application's point of view until the moment it's promoted. A team that enables Multi-AZ expecting it to also relieve read load on the primary has misread what the feature does; that's precisely the job of read replicas, covered next, which is a separate feature addressing a separate problem, even though both involve running additional copies of your data.

sections.heading: Read Replicas: Scaling Read Throughput, Asynchronously
sections.body:
A **read replica** is a separate RDS instance that receives data asynchronously (not synchronously, unlike a Multi-AZ standby) from a source database, and unlike a Multi-AZ standby, a read replica *can* serve live read queries -- that's its entire purpose. Applications with read-heavy workloads can point some fraction of their read traffic (reporting queries, analytics, read-only API endpoints) at one or more read replicas instead of the primary, freeing up the primary's capacity for writes and for reads that genuinely need up-to-the-millisecond freshness.

Because replication to a read replica is asynchronous, there is **replication lag** -- a small, variable delay between a write completing on the primary and that same data becoming visible on a given replica, typically milliseconds under normal conditions but capable of growing under heavy write load or replica resource contention. This makes read replicas a poor fit for any read that must see a write it just performed an instant earlier (a user submitting a form and immediately being redirected to a page that reads back what they just wrote is a classic case where reading from a lagging replica can show stale data) -- that specific read pattern belongs on the primary, or requires an application-level strategy to tolerate or route around the lag. Read replicas can also, for some engines, be promoted to become a fully independent, standalone database, which is a useful tool for splitting off a workload entirely or for disaster-recovery scenarios distinct from Multi-AZ's automated same-Region failover -- notably, a read replica can even be created in a *different* Region than its source, which Multi-AZ standbys cannot do, making cross-Region read replicas a genuinely different tool for a genuinely different kind of resilience than in-Region Multi-AZ failover.

sections.heading: Backups and Point-in-Time Recovery: What They Actually Restore, and How Far Back
sections.body:
RDS automated backups take a daily full snapshot of the database plus continuously captured transaction logs, and together these enable **point-in-time recovery (PITR)** -- the ability to restore the database to its exact state at any specific second within the configured retention window (up to 35 days), not just to the moment of the most recent daily snapshot. This distinction matters concretely during an incident: if a bad deployment or an accidental `DELETE` without a `WHERE` clause corrupts data at 2:17pm, PITR lets you restore to 2:16pm specifically, rather than losing an entire day's worth of legitimate writes by rolling back to last night's snapshot.

A detail worth being precise about, because it's a common source of a bad surprise during an actual incident: a PITR restore does not modify the existing database in place -- it creates a **new** RDS instance at the recovered point in time, with a new endpoint. Recovering from a bad write means restoring to a new instance, verifying the data there, and then redirecting the application to the new instance (or exporting and re-applying the specific corrected data), not an in-place undo on the database currently serving traffic. Automated backups also have a real, finite retention window -- up to 35 days for RDS's automated backups -- so any longer-term retention requirement (regulatory retention rules, year-over-year archival) needs manual or automated **snapshots** taken and retained deliberately, since automated backups alone are not a substitute for a longer archival policy.

sections.heading: What Still Isn't RDS's Job: Schema, Queries, Sizing, and Access Control
sections.body:
It's worth closing the loop explicitly on where RDS's automation stops, because the failure mode of assuming a managed service has quietly taken over more than it actually has is a recurring theme across this whole module. RDS does not design your schema, does not choose your indexes, and will run a poorly written query or an unindexed table scan exactly as slowly as a self-managed database would -- query and schema performance is entirely on the 'in the cloud' side of the responsibility line, unaffected by how much of the underlying infrastructure AWS manages. RDS does not automatically size your instance correctly for your workload either -- an undersized instance class will bottleneck on CPU, memory, or IOPS regardless of how well-patched and well-backed-up it is, and choosing the right instance class and storage configuration for actual load is squarely a customer decision, exactly analogous to the EC2 instance-family sizing decision covered earlier in this subject.

Access control is the same story: RDS integrates with IAM for *administrative* actions (creating, modifying, deleting a database instance) and optionally for authentication to the database itself via IAM database authentication, but the database's own internal user/permission model (`GRANT`/`REVOKE` at the SQL level, or the equivalent for a given engine) is entirely your responsibility to design and maintain correctly, exactly as it would be on a self-managed database. A database exposed on a security group that's too permissive, or a database user granted broader privileges than an application actually needs, is precisely the kind of 'in the cloud' misconfiguration that RDS's operational automation does nothing to prevent -- the managed service took the patching and failover mechanics off your plate, not the responsibility for configuring access correctly.

examples.title: Creating a Multi-AZ RDS Instance and Adding a Read Replica
examples.code:
# A Multi-AZ primary -- the standby is created and kept in sync automatically,
# but is not available for read queries
aws rds create-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier orders-db \
  --engine postgres \
  --db-instance-class db.r6g.large \
  --allocated-storage 100 \
  --multi-az \
  --master-username admin \
  --master-user-password '**********'

# A read replica of that same database, usable for live read queries,
# receiving data asynchronously with some replication lag
aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica \
  --db-instance-identifier orders-db-read-1 \
  --source-db-instance-identifier orders-db
examples.explanation: These two commands create two structurally different things that are easy to conflate because both involve 'another copy of the database.' The `--multi-az` flag on the primary's creation gives it a synchronously replicated standby purely for automated failover -- that standby cannot be queried directly and contributes nothing to read capacity. `create-db-instance-read-replica` creates an entirely separate, independently addressable instance (`orders-db-read-1`, with its own endpoint) that an application can actually send read queries to, asynchronously kept in sync with the source. A team that runs only the first command and then wonders why their read-heavy dashboard queries are still bottlenecked on the primary has correctly set up availability protection but hasn't touched read scalability at all -- the two commands solve two different problems, and running one doesn't substitute for the other.

examples.title: Point-in-Time Recovery After a Bad Write
examples.code:
# A bad deployment ran an UPDATE without a WHERE clause at 14:17 UTC,
# corrupting the orders table. Restore to just before that moment --
# NOTE: this creates a brand-new instance, it does not modify orders-db in place.
aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time \
  --source-db-instance-identifier orders-db \
  --target-db-instance-identifier orders-db-restored-14-16 \
  --restore-time 2026-08-14T14:16:00Z
examples.explanation: This command produces a new RDS instance, `orders-db-restored-14-16`, reconstructed from the automated backup and transaction logs to reflect exactly how `orders-db` looked at 14:16:00 UTC -- one minute before the bad update ran. The original `orders-db` instance is completely untouched by this command and keeps running and serving traffic exactly as it was, including the corrupted data, for however long it takes to verify the restored instance and decide what to do next (redirect the application to the new instance, or selectively copy the corrected rows back). This is exactly the detail from the explanation worth internalizing before an actual incident, rather than during one under pressure: point-in-time recovery is a 'create a new, correct instance next to the broken one' operation, not an in-place time-travel undo button on the database currently in production.

examples.title: A Correctly-Sized Instance Still Bottlenecked by a Missing Index
examples.code:
-- orders table: 40 million rows, no index on customer_id
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 48213;

-- Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..812000.00 rows=40000000)
--   Filter: (customer_id = 48213)
--   Execution Time: 4210.331 ms

-- After: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 48213;

-- Index Scan using idx_orders_customer_id on orders  (cost=0.43..8.45 rows=12)
--   Index Cond: (customer_id = 48213)
--   Execution Time: 0.412 ms
examples.explanation: This query runs on a properly sized, Multi-AZ, automatically backed-up RDS instance -- every operational box RDS is responsible for is checked. And yet the first version takes over 4 seconds, because PostgreSQL has no index to use and has to scan all 40 million rows to find the matching ones, a `Seq Scan` that RDS's management of patching and failover has no bearing on whatsoever. Adding the index drops execution time to under half a millisecond -- a roughly 10,000x improvement -- achieved entirely through schema/index design, a responsibility that sits on the customer's side of the line no matter which database platform (RDS, self-managed EC2, or anything else) is running the query. This is exactly the concrete case the explanation is pointing at: RDS's operational automation and query performance are almost entirely independent axes, and being excellent on one says nothing about the other.

misconceptions.description: Enabling Multi-AZ on an RDS instance improves read performance by letting the application spread queries across the primary and the standby.
misconceptions.clarification: A Multi-AZ standby exists purely as a synchronously replicated failover target and cannot serve read queries at all during normal operation -- it sits idle, from an application's perspective, until the moment RDS promotes it after detecting a primary failure. Spreading read queries across multiple instances requires read replicas, a separate feature that creates additional, independently queryable instances kept in sync asynchronously. Enabling Multi-AZ addresses availability; it does nothing for read throughput.

misconceptions.description: Because RDS handles patching, backups, and failover automatically, a team no longer needs to think about database performance or access control -- those are 'AWS's problem' once the database is on RDS.
misconceptions.clarification: RDS automates the operational mechanics of running the database engine -- OS patching, engine version updates, backup scheduling, failover orchestration -- but schema design, query and index performance, instance sizing for actual load, and access control (both IAM for administrative actions and the database's own internal user/permission model) remain entirely the customer's responsibility, identical to what they'd own on a self-managed database. A poorly indexed query or an overly permissive database user is exactly as much of a real problem on RDS as it would be anywhere else; RDS's automation covers infrastructure operations, not application-level correctness or performance.

exercises.prompt: A team enabled Multi-AZ on their production RDS instance specifically to fix slow response times on their read-heavy reporting dashboard, reasoning that the standby instance could absorb some of that read load. Response times haven't improved at all. Diagnose why, and propose the actual fix.
exercises.code:
current_setup:
  db_instance: orders-db
  multi_az: true          # enabled specifically hoping to offload read traffic
  read_replicas: []       # none configured
  symptom: "reporting dashboard queries still slow, no change after enabling Multi-AZ"
hints: What is a Multi-AZ standby actually available for during normal operation -- can an application send it read queries at all?
The feature that creates an additional, independently queryable copy of the data for read traffic is a different RDS feature entirely from Multi-AZ.
Consider also whether reporting/dashboard queries specifically need up-to-the-second freshness, or whether they could tolerate the small replication lag that comes with the correct fix.
exercises.solutionCode:
fixed_setup:
  db_instance: orders-db
  multi_az: true                     # keep -- this still correctly protects availability
  read_replicas: ["orders-db-read-1"]  # add -- this is what actually offloads read traffic
  dashboard_queries_routed_to: "orders-db-read-1"
exercises.solutionExplanation: Multi-AZ's standby instance is never available to serve query traffic during normal operation -- it exists solely as a synchronously replicated failover target, so enabling it changes nothing about read capacity or read latency, which is exactly why the dashboard saw no improvement. The correct fix is to add a read replica, a separate RDS feature that creates an additional, independently addressable instance receiving data asynchronously, and then point the reporting dashboard's queries specifically at that replica's endpoint instead of the primary's. Multi-AZ should stay enabled -- it's still doing its own separate job of protecting availability against an AZ or instance failure -- but it was never going to solve a read-throughput problem, because that was never the problem it was designed to address.

exercises.prompt: At 09:00 UTC, a deploy script accidentally runs an UPDATE that corrupts pricing data across an entire product catalog table. The team notices at 09:45 UTC and immediately runs a point-in-time-recovery restore targeting 08:59 UTC. Describe exactly what state the production system is in immediately after that restore command completes, and what manual steps (if any) remain before the corrupted data is actually fixed for real users.
exercises.code:
timeline:
  09:00 UTC: bad UPDATE runs, corrupting pricing data
  09:45 UTC: team notices, initiates PITR restore targeting 08:59 UTC
  restore command: aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time --source-db-instance-identifier catalog-db --target-db-instance-identifier catalog-db-restored --restore-time 2026-08-14T08:59:00Z
hints: PITR restores create a new instance rather than modifying the existing one in place -- what is catalog-db (the original, currently-serving instance) doing throughout this whole process?
The new instance, catalog-db-restored, has correct pricing data as of 08:59 UTC -- but is it the instance real users' traffic is actually reaching right after the restore command finishes?
Think about what legitimate writes (new orders, inventory changes, etc.) might have happened on catalog-db between 08:59 and 09:45 that also aren't reflected on the restored instance.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Immediately after the restore command completes, catalog-db (the original instance) is still running and still serving live production traffic, with the corrupted pricing data from the 09:00 UPDATE still present -- the restore command did not touch it. A new, separate instance, catalog-db-restored, now exists with correct pricing data as of 08:59 UTC, but nothing is pointed at it yet. Real users are not yet seeing correct data. Manual steps remain: verify catalog-db-restored has the expected correct data, reconcile any legitimate writes that happened between 08:59 and 09:45 (which exist on catalog-db but not on the restored instance) so they aren't lost, and then either redirect the application to catalog-db-restored or selectively copy the corrected pricing rows back into catalog-db.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The key fact driving this whole scenario is that `restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time` always creates a brand-new RDS instance rather than modifying the source instance in place -- so the instant the restore command finishes, there are simply two databases: the original `catalog-db`, unchanged and still serving traffic with the corrupted pricing data intact, and the new `catalog-db-restored`, containing a faithful snapshot of everything as of 08:59 UTC. Nothing about running the restore command automatically redirects any traffic, which is precisely why real users are still seeing the corrupted state immediately afterward -- the restore produced a correct *copy* of the data, not a live fix. The 46-minute gap between 08:59 and 09:45 also matters: any legitimate order or inventory change made on `catalog-db` during that window exists there but not on `catalog-db-restored`, so a full cutover without reconciling that gap would silently lose real, valid data alongside discarding the corruption -- which is exactly why 'restore and immediately redirect everything' is rarely the complete fix; verifying the restored data and reconciling the gap window are real, necessary manual steps, not a formality.

assessments.prompt: A team's RDS-hosted application is experiencing slow read query performance during peak hours, and a review shows the primary instance's CPU is consistently near 100% due to heavy analytical reporting queries mixed in with normal transactional traffic. Which RDS feature most directly addresses this specific bottleneck?
options: Enabling Multi-AZ, so the standby instance can absorb some of the reporting query load.
Adding one or more read replicas and routing the analytical reporting queries to them, leaving the primary free for transactional traffic.
Increasing the automated backup retention period to capture more historical data for reporting purposes.
Switching the database engine from the current engine to a different one, since engine choice determines CPU capacity.
assessments.explanation: The bottleneck described -- primary CPU saturated by a mix of transactional and analytical query load -- is precisely what read replicas are built to relieve: routing the analytical/reporting queries to one or more replicas frees the primary's CPU for transactional traffic, at the cost of the replicas' data lagging the primary by a small, usually tolerable amount, which is generally acceptable for reporting use cases. Option A is the classic Multi-AZ misconception -- a standby cannot serve any query traffic at all during normal operation, so it does nothing for this bottleneck. Option C confuses backup retention (how far back you can restore to) with query capacity, which are unrelated. Option D is a red herring -- CPU capacity is a function of instance class/size, not which relational engine is running, and switching engines is a disproportionate, unrelated response to a workload-distribution problem.

assessments.prompt: During an RDS Multi-AZ failover, the database's DNS endpoint automatically updates to point at the newly promoted standby, with the whole process typically completing within roughly 60-120 seconds. Given this, what should application code do to handle a failover gracefully?
options: Nothing; failover is instantaneous and completely invisible to any application already connected to the database.
Manually reconfigure the application's connection string to a new endpoint once failover completes, since the DNS endpoint does not update on its own.

Implement connection retry logic to handle the brief connection interruption during the failover window, since although the endpoint itself doesn't need to change, an in-progress connection is disrupted while the standby is being promoted.
Switch the application to use a read replica's endpoint instead of the primary's, since only read replicas remain reachable during a Multi-AZ failover.
assessments.explanation: RDS handles the DNS endpoint update automatically during Multi-AZ failover, so the application never needs a new connection string -- but that doesn't mean the failover is invisible: an existing connection is disrupted while the standby is promoted, and reaching the database again requires reconnecting, which is exactly why building in retry logic rather than assuming instantaneous continuity matters. Option A overstates the guarantee -- there's a real, if brief, disruption window. Option B is wrong because the DNS endpoint update is automatic, not manual. Option D confuses read replicas (a separate feature for read scaling) with the Multi-AZ standby itself, which is what actually gets promoted during this specific failover.

assessments.prompt: A user submits a form that writes a new record to the primary RDS instance, and the application immediately redirects them to a page that reads that same record back from a read replica. What is the most likely risk, and why?
options: There is no risk; read replicas are updated synchronously, so the new record is guaranteed to be visible immediately.

The read might not find the record yet, or might see a stale version of it, because replication to a read replica is asynchronous, introducing replication lag between when a write completes on the primary and when it becomes visible on that replica.
The read will fail outright, since read replicas cannot serve any read traffic for the first several seconds after any write occurs anywhere in the database.
This is only a risk if Multi-AZ happens to also be enabled on the same primary instance.
assessments.explanation: Read replicas receive data asynchronously, unlike a Multi-AZ standby's synchronous replication, which means there's a small, variable replication lag between a write completing on the primary and that write becoming visible on a given replica. A read-your-own-write pattern -- writing to the primary and immediately reading from a replica -- is exactly the case where that lag can surface as a visible bug, showing stale or missing data. Option A incorrectly attributes synchronous replication to read replicas, which is the Multi-AZ standby's behavior, not a read replica's. Option C invents an outright failure mode that doesn't reflect how replication lag actually behaves -- reads still succeed, they just may return stale data. Option D incorrectly ties this risk to Multi-AZ, which is an unrelated, separate feature.

assessments.prompt: A company needs to retain the ability to restore their RDS database to any specific point in time within the last 2 years, for a regulatory retention requirement. Is RDS's automated backup and point-in-time recovery feature sufficient for this on its own?
options: Yes, automated backups and point-in-time recovery support an effectively unlimited retention window by default.

No -- automated backups' point-in-time recovery window has a maximum retention of up to 35 days; a 2-year requirement needs manual or automated snapshots taken and retained deliberately as a separate, longer-term archival strategy.
Yes, as long as Multi-AZ is enabled, since the standby instance retains historical data indefinitely.
No, because RDS provides no backup or recovery capability of any kind beyond whatever a read replica happens to retain.
assessments.explanation: RDS's automated backups and point-in-time recovery have a real, finite retention window -- up to 35 days -- so a 2-year regulatory requirement is well beyond what that feature alone provides. Meeting a longer-term retention need requires manual or automated snapshots taken and retained deliberately as a separate archival policy, since automated backups aren't designed as a substitute for long-term archival. Option A overstates the retention window, which is explicitly capped. Option C incorrectly attributes indefinite historical retention to the Multi-AZ standby, which only mirrors current data for failover purposes and isn't a historical archive. Option D understates RDS's real, genuine backup capability, which does exist -- it's just capped well short of 2 years.

assessments.prompt: A junior engineer says, 'We moved our database to RDS, so we don't really need to worry about database performance or security anymore -- AWS manages it.' Explain what's accurate and what's mistaken in that statement, being specific about where the actual dividing line falls.
assessments.modelAnswer: The accurate part of the statement is real and worth crediting: RDS genuinely takes over a substantial category of operational work that would otherwise be the team's responsibility on a self-managed database -- patching the guest operating system (which RDS users never even get direct access to), applying engine version updates on a configured schedule, automating daily backups and transaction-log capture for point-in-time recovery, and orchestrating the mechanics of failover for a Multi-AZ deployment. None of that requires the team to write or maintain any operational tooling themselves, and that's a genuine, meaningful reduction in burden. The mistaken part is treating 'AWS manages the infrastructure' as equivalent to 'AWS manages our outcomes.' Schema design and query/index performance are entirely untouched by any of RDS's automation -- an unindexed query scanning forty million rows runs exactly as slowly on a perfectly patched, perfectly backed-up RDS instance as it would anywhere else, because that's a property of the schema and the query, not the infrastructure underneath them. Instance sizing is the same story: RDS will run whatever instance class is selected, but it doesn't decide whether that class is actually sufficient for the real workload, and an undersized instance bottlenecks on CPU, memory, or IOPS regardless of how well-managed its patching is. Security follows the identical pattern: RDS integrates with IAM for administrative actions and can support IAM-based database authentication, but the database's own internal grant/permission model, and the security groups controlling network access to the instance, are entirely the team's own configuration to get right -- an overly permissive database user or an open security group is exactly as real a vulnerability on RDS as on a self-managed instance, and RDS's operational automation does nothing to catch or prevent it. The accurate way to state the situation is that RDS moved a specific, well-defined category of work -- infrastructure operations -- onto AWS's side of the line, without moving schema design, query performance, instance sizing, or access control off the team's side at all; those remain exactly as much the team's job, and exactly as consequential if done poorly, as they would be with a fully self-managed database.

concepts.title: DynamoDB Basics: Keys, Partitions, and NoSQL Scaling
concepts.description: DynamoDB stores items addressed by a key rather than rows related through joins, and its partition key is the single design decision that determines whether the table scales smoothly to massive throughput or concentrates traffic onto one overloaded partition -- which is why DynamoDB rewards designing access patterns up front in a way relational databases don't require.
learningObjectives: Explain DynamoDB's item/attribute data model and contrast it with a relational table's rows and columns, including why DynamoDB has no joins.
Explain what a partition key is, how DynamoDB uses it to distribute data and throughput, and why key choice directly determines scalability.
Diagnose a 'hot partition' problem from its symptoms and propose a partition key redesign that fixes it.
Distinguish a simple primary key from a composite primary key (partition key + sort key) and explain what a sort key enables.
Explain why DynamoDB scales differently from a relational database -- specifically, why it doesn't get slower as a single table grows, provided the partition key is well-chosen.

sections.heading: Items and Attributes, Not Rows and Columns -- and No Joins
sections.body:
A DynamoDB table stores **items**, and each item is a collection of **attributes** -- conceptually similar to a JSON document, and in fact DynamoDB natively supports nested lists and maps as attribute values, not just flat scalar fields. Unlike a relational table, items in the same DynamoDB table don't need to share the same set of attributes at all: one item might have five attributes and the next item in the same table might have a completely different eight, with no schema migration required to accommodate the difference, because DynamoDB doesn't enforce a fixed schema beyond the key attributes that identify each item.

The more consequential difference, though, is that **DynamoDB has no joins**, and this isn't a missing feature so much as a deliberate design constraint that shapes everything else about how you use it. A relational database lets you normalize data across multiple tables and reassemble it at query time with a `JOIN`; DynamoDB expects you to model your data so that everything a specific access pattern needs can be retrieved from a single table (often even a single item, or a small, predictable set of items under one partition key) with a single request, because there is no query-time mechanism to combine data from multiple items the way a join combines rows. This pushes a real amount of design work earlier in the process than a relational schema requires: with DynamoDB, you're expected to know your application's actual access patterns -- which specific queries you'll run, and how frequently -- *before* you finalize your table and key design, denormalizing and duplicating data deliberately where needed so that each access pattern maps to an efficient, joinless read. Arriving at DynamoDB with a relational mindset and trying to normalize data the way you would in Postgres or MySQL, then wondering how to 'join' it back together at query time, is one of the most common and most frustrating early missteps for teams new to the service.

sections.heading: The Partition Key: What Actually Determines Scalability
sections.body:
Every DynamoDB table has a **partition key** (sometimes called a hash key), and DynamoDB uses it to decide, deterministically, which physical storage partition a given item lives on -- the key's value is run through an internal hash function, and the result determines placement. This single mechanism is the entire basis of DynamoDB's ability to scale to very large request volumes: as a table's total traffic grows, DynamoDB can add more partitions behind the scenes and spread the read/write load across all of them, provided that load is actually spread across many *distinct partition key values* to begin with.

That last clause is the crucial, easy-to-miss catch, and it's the source of the single most common DynamoDB design mistake: a **hot partition**. If a large share of a table's traffic concentrates on a small number of partition key values -- a status field with only three possible values (`"pending"`, `"active"`, `"closed"`) used as the partition key, for instance, or a single well-known tenant ID that accounts for a disproportionate share of all traffic -- then no matter how many partitions the underlying table has been split into overall, that specific overrepresented key's traffic is still confined to whichever one partition its value happens to hash to. Requests against that one partition get throttled once they exceed that partition's own individual throughput ceiling, even while the table's *aggregate* configured or on-demand capacity looks nowhere close to exhausted -- a confusing symptom, because dashboards showing table-wide metrics can look perfectly healthy while a specific access pattern is being throttled hard. The fix is choosing (or reshaping) the partition key so that traffic is genuinely spread across a large number of distinct values that actually appear with roughly even frequency in real traffic -- a customer ID or an order ID, for a workload with many customers or many orders, is a far better partition key than a small, low-cardinality status field, precisely because it naturally distributes across many partitions instead of concentrating onto a handful.

sections.heading: Composite Primary Keys: Adding a Sort Key
sections.body:
A table can define either a **simple primary key** (the partition key alone, uniquely identifying each item) or a **composite primary key** (a partition key plus a **sort key**), and the sort key adds real query capability, not just a second identifying field. Within a single partition key value, items are physically stored sorted by their sort key, which means a query for 'all items with this partition key, where the sort key falls in this range' is efficient and native to DynamoDB -- no scan required.

A very common real pattern uses this directly: a table with partition key `customerId` and sort key `orderDate#orderId` lets you fetch all orders for one customer sorted chronologically, or all orders for one customer within a specific date range, with a single efficient `Query` call -- the composite key structure is doing the work a relational `WHERE customer_id = ? AND order_date BETWEEN ? AND ?` with an index would do, but expressed through key design rather than a separate index built after the fact (though DynamoDB does also support genuinely separate **secondary indexes**, both global and local, for access patterns that don't fit the table's primary key structure at all -- covered further in more advanced material, but worth knowing exists as an escape hatch when a single primary key structure can't serve every access pattern the application needs). Without a sort key, a table can only ever fetch one item at a time by its exact, unique partition key value -- there's no notion of 'a range of items under the same partition key' at all, since there's nothing distinguishing items within that key beyond the key itself.

sections.heading: Why DynamoDB Scales Differently From a Relational Database
sections.body:
A well-designed DynamoDB table's read and write latency for a given operation stays roughly constant regardless of how large the table grows overall -- fetching a single item by its exact primary key takes about the same time whether the table holds a thousand items or a hundred billion, because DynamoDB routes the request directly to the specific partition that item lives on, without scanning or searching through unrelated data. This is a fundamentally different scaling story from a relational database, where an unindexed query's cost grows with the *total* size of the table being scanned (recall the sequential-scan example from the RDS concept, where a 40-million-row table without the right index took over four seconds) -- indexes mitigate that in a relational database, but DynamoDB's model achieves the same property more directly, by using the partition key itself as the addressing mechanism for every single request, not as an optional optimization layered on top of an otherwise scannable table.

The trade-off behind that property is exactly what the earlier sections built up to: this speed and scalability is available specifically for queries that go through the partition key (and, within a partition, the sort key) -- a request that doesn't specify the partition key at all, and instead wants to filter on some other attribute across the whole table, requires a `Scan` operation that reads through a large portion or all of the table's items, which is slow and expensive at scale in exactly the way a relational full-table scan is, and which DynamoDB explicitly warns against relying on for a table of any real size. This is the direct payoff of the earlier point about designing around access patterns up front: a table modeled around the actual queries the application runs gets uniformly fast, scale-independent performance; a table queried in ways its key structure wasn't designed for falls back to the same scanning cost profile DynamoDB was specifically built to avoid.

examples.title: Modeling One Access Pattern With a Composite Key
examples.explanation: The sort key `ORDER#2026-08-01#O-9911` deliberately embeds the order date at the front, before the order's own ID -- this is a common DynamoDB modeling technique specifically so that a range condition on the sort key (via `begins_with`, or a `BETWEEN` on a full date range) naturally expresses 'orders in this date range,' since items under the same partition key are physically stored sorted by their sort key value. This single item, retrieved via one efficient `Query`, contains everything this specific access pattern needs -- there's no second table to join against for order line items, because they're embedded directly as a nested list attribute rather than normalized into a separate table the way a relational schema would likely split them out. This is the denormalization the earlier explanation described: the data is shaped around the specific 'fetch a customer's orders in a date range, with their line items' access pattern, not around a normalized, join-friendly relational structure.

examples.title: A Hot Partition, Diagnosed From Symptoms
examples.code:
Table: Jobs   partition key: status   (values: "pending", "processing", "done")

CloudWatch metrics:
  Table-level ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits: well within provisioned capacity
  ThrottledRequests for partition key "pending":  spiking heavily
  ThrottledRequests for partition key "done":     near zero

Symptom: workers polling for status="pending" jobs get throttled constantly,
while the table's overall metrics look healthy.
examples.explanation: This is the hot-partition symptom described in the explanation, made concrete: the partition key here is `status`, which only ever takes on three distinct values across the entire table, no matter how large the table grows. Every single 'pending' job -- potentially millions of them under real load -- lives on whichever one physical partition the string `"pending"` happens to hash to, and that one partition has its own individual throughput ceiling completely independent of the table's aggregate provisioned or on-demand capacity. The table-wide metrics look fine precisely because the *aggregate* traffic across all partitions (including the much lighter `"done"` traffic) is well within overall capacity -- the problem is entirely concentrated on one partition that dashboards showing table-wide totals don't surface clearly. The fix is a different partition key entirely -- something with much higher cardinality, like `jobId`, with `status` moved to a regular attribute (queried via a secondary index if 'all pending jobs' needs to remain an efficient query) -- so that job traffic spreads across many partitions instead of collapsing onto three.

examples.title: The Same Table Queried Correctly vs. Via an Expensive Scan
examples.explanation: Both operations can return correct results, but their cost profiles are entirely different, and that difference is the direct consequence of whether the operation is routed by the partition key or not. The `Query` goes straight to the one partition holding `CUST#48213`'s items, so its cost is a function of how much data that one customer has, not how large the `Orders` table is overall -- exactly the scale-independence described in the explanation. The `Scan` has no partition key to route by at all; DynamoDB has to examine a broad swath of the table's items to evaluate `total > 100` against each one, and that cost grows with the table's total size, not with how many items actually satisfy the filter -- a `Scan` returning only a handful of matching items out of a hundred-million-item table still pays roughly the cost of examining that much of the table. This is precisely why 'design around your access patterns up front' matters so concretely: an access pattern that maps to a `Query` gets DynamoDB's core scaling promise, and one that only maps to a `Scan` gets a cost profile the service was specifically designed to help you avoid.

misconceptions.description: Since DynamoDB is a NoSQL/document database, the choice of partition key is mostly a stylistic preference, similar to picking which column to use as a primary key in a relational table.
misconceptions.clarification: The partition key choice directly determines how DynamoDB physically distributes an item's data and throughput across its underlying partitions, and it is the single biggest factor in whether a table scales smoothly or develops a hot partition. A low-cardinality partition key (one with only a handful of distinct values actually appearing in real traffic) concentrates a disproportionate share of requests onto very few physical partitions, each with its own individual throughput ceiling, regardless of the table's overall provisioned or on-demand capacity -- this is a scalability decision with real operational consequences, not a stylistic one comparable to choosing a relational primary key column.

misconceptions.description: DynamoDB tables should be modeled the same way relational tables are -- normalize related data into separate tables, then join or query across them as needed at read time.
misconceptions.clarification: DynamoDB has no join operation at all, and its performance model specifically rewards designing a table (or a small number of tables) around the application's actual known access patterns up front, denormalizing and duplicating data deliberately so that each access pattern can be satisfied from a single table, often with a single Query, without needing to combine data from multiple items or tables at query time. Arriving with a relational normalization mindset and expecting to reassemble related data across tables at query time leads to needing multiple round trips or falling back to expensive Scan operations that DynamoDB's model is specifically built to help you avoid.

exercises.prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS application stores usage events in a DynamoDB table with partition key tenantTier (values: "free", "pro", "enterprise"). One giant enterprise customer generates the overwhelming majority of all events in the system. The team is seeing throttled writes specifically for enterprise-tier events, even though the table's overall provisioned capacity metrics look far from exhausted. Diagnose the root cause and propose a partition key redesign.
exercises.code:
table: UsageEvents
partition_key: tenantTier   # "free" | "pro" | "enterprise"
symptom: "enterprise-tier writes throttled heavily; table-wide capacity metrics look healthy"
context: "one very large enterprise customer accounts for most of all events system-wide"
hints: How many distinct values can tenantTier ever actually take across the whole table, no matter how many tenants or events exist?

Every item with tenantTier = "enterprise" -- across every enterprise customer, including the one dominant one -- hashes to the exact same physical partition, regardless of how much total provisioned capacity the table has.
The fix needs a partition key with much higher cardinality that still supports the application's actual access patterns -- consider using something tenant-specific rather than tier-specific.
exercises.solutionCode:
table: UsageEvents
partition_key: tenantId    # one distinct value per tenant, much higher cardinality
sort_key: eventTimestamp#eventId
# tenantTier moves to a regular (non-key) attribute, queryable via a
# secondary index if "all enterprise-tier events across tenants" is
# still a needed access pattern
exercises.solutionExplanation: `tenantTier` only ever has three possible values in this table, so every single item -- across every tenant that happens to share a tier -- hashes to one of only three physical partitions, and one giant enterprise customer's traffic is entirely confined to whichever single partition `"enterprise"` hashes to, no matter how much total capacity the table has been provisioned with overall. That's a textbook hot partition: the throttling is real and specific to that one partition's own throughput ceiling, even while table-wide metrics (which aggregate across all partitions, including the much lighter `"free"` and `"pro"` traffic) look healthy. Switching the partition key to `tenantId` gives every distinct tenant, including the large enterprise one, its own dedicated partition-key value, so traffic is distributed by actual tenant rather than collapsed onto three tier buckets -- the dominant enterprise tenant still generates a lot of traffic, but it's now isolated to its own partition rather than sharing one partition's throughput ceiling with every other enterprise-tier tenant combined. If 'all enterprise-tier events across every tenant' is still a genuinely needed query, that access pattern would now go through a secondary index on the `tenantTier` attribute rather than through the primary key, since the primary key's job has shifted to optimizing for the far more common per-tenant access pattern.

exercises.prompt: Design a partition key and sort key for a DynamoDB table storing chat messages, given this single required access pattern: fetch all messages in a specific chat room, ordered from oldest to newest, optionally limited to a specific date range. Write the key schema and a short example item, then explain why this schema satisfies the access pattern efficiently.
hints: The partition key should be whatever the access pattern always filters down to first -- what does every relevant query have in common ("messages in a specific ___")?
The sort key needs to support ordering AND range filtering by date -- what value, placed at the front of the sort key, makes both of those possible via begins_with or a BETWEEN condition?

Make sure the partition key has enough distinct values across the whole table (many chat rooms) to avoid concentrating traffic onto too few partitions, unlike the tenantTier mistake from the previous exercise.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `roomId` is the partition key because it's exactly what the required access pattern always filters down to first -- 'messages in a specific chat room' -- and because a real application has many, many chat rooms, this key has high cardinality and spreads traffic across many partitions rather than concentrating it, avoiding the hot-partition mistake from the previous exercise. The sort key, `sentAt#messageId`, puts an ISO-8601 timestamp at the front specifically so that items under the same `roomId` are physically stored in chronological order, which is exactly what 'ordered from oldest to newest' requires with no extra sorting step, and it makes a date-range restriction a direct `BETWEEN` condition on the sort key rather than something requiring a filter pass over unrelated items. The `messageId` suffix exists purely to guarantee uniqueness in case two messages in the same room land on the identical timestamp, which a pure timestamp sort key alone couldn't guarantee. This schema satisfies the one stated access pattern with a single, efficient `Query` -- because that access pattern was designed into the key structure from the start, exactly the DynamoDB modeling discipline the explanation described, rather than being bolted on afterward with a scan or a secondary index.

assessments.prompt: A DynamoDB table's write requests are being throttled for one specific, very common partition key value, even though CloudWatch shows the table's overall consumed capacity well below its provisioned or on-demand limits. What does this most strongly indicate?
options: The table's total item count has exceeded a hard DynamoDB size limit and needs to be split into multiple tables.

A hot partition: too much traffic is concentrated on that one partition key value, exceeding that specific partition's own throughput ceiling even though aggregate table-wide capacity is not exhausted.
DynamoDB is experiencing a regional outage affecting only that specific key value.
The sort key is missing from the table, which is required for DynamoDB to distribute any table's write load.
assessments.explanation: Table-wide capacity metrics looking healthy while one specific key value's requests are throttled is the defining symptom of a hot partition: DynamoDB distributes items and throughput across partitions based on the partition key's hashed value, and every item sharing that one overrepresented key value lands on the same physical partition, which has its own individual throughput ceiling independent of the table's aggregate capacity. Option A invents a size-based limit that isn't the actual mechanism here -- this is a distribution problem, not a total-size problem. Option C fabricates a per-key outage, which isn't how DynamoDB throttling works. Option D is incorrect because a sort key is optional and orthogonal to load distribution -- distribution across partitions is entirely a function of the partition key, not whether a sort key exists.

assessments.prompt: A table has partition key customerId and sort key orderDate#orderId. If this table had only a simple primary key (customerId alone, with no sort key), what specific capability would it lose?
options: The ability to store more than one non-key attribute on each item.

The ability to fetch a range of items sharing the same partition key value -- such as all of one customer's orders within a date range -- in a single efficient query; without a sort key, a partition key value can only ever address one uniquely identified item.
The ability for the table to distribute items across more than one physical partition at all.
The ability to choose between provisioned and on-demand capacity modes for the table.
assessments.explanation: A sort key's specific contribution is enabling multiple items to share the same partition key value while remaining individually addressable and range-queryable, since items within a partition are physically stored sorted by their sort key. Without one, a partition key value maps to exactly one item, with no notion of 'a range of items under this key' at all -- fetching a customer's orders in a date range would have no way to be expressed as a single efficient request. Option A is unrelated -- attribute count per item has nothing to do with sort keys. Option C is wrong -- partition distribution is governed by the partition key alone, independent of whether a sort key exists. Option D is also unrelated -- capacity mode is a separate table-level setting with no connection to key schema.

assessments.prompt: A DynamoDB table grows from 1 million to 100 million items. A Query using one customer's exact partition key, and a Scan filtering on a non-key attribute across the whole table, are each run before and after this growth. What happens to each operation's latency?
options: Both operations get proportionally slower, since DynamoDB latency is always a direct function of total table size regardless of which operation is used.

The Query's latency stays roughly the same, since it's routed directly to the one partition holding that customer's items regardless of the table's total size; the Scan's latency grows substantially, since it has to examine a portion of the table proportional to the table's new, much larger size.
Both operations get faster, since DynamoDB automatically adding more partitions as a table grows uniformly speeds up every kind of read, including Scans.
The Query becomes slower while the Scan's latency stays constant, since Scans always execute against a fixed-size sample regardless of table size.
assessments.explanation: A Query addressed by the exact partition key is routed directly to the specific partition holding that data, so its cost is a function of how much data lives under that one key, not the table's overall size -- this is the scale-independence DynamoDB is specifically designed to provide for key-addressed access. A Scan has no partition key to route by, so it must examine a portion of the table proportional to its total size to evaluate the filter, meaning its cost grows as the table grows, independent of how few items actually match. Option A incorrectly generalizes the Scan's size-dependent cost to the Query as well. Option C invents a uniform speedup that doesn't apply to Scans, which read broadly regardless of partition count. Option D reverses which operation is size-independent.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a developer coming from a relational database background why DynamoDB requires knowing your access patterns before finalizing a table design, in a way relational schema design typically doesn't -- and connect this directly to why partition key choice matters so much.
assessments.modelAnswer: A relational database lets you design a normalized schema largely independent of the specific queries you'll eventually run against it, because the query engine can reassemble normalized data at read time using joins, and can use indexes added after the fact to make a wide variety of query shapes reasonably efficient without redesigning the underlying tables. DynamoDB removes that flexibility deliberately: there is no join operation at all, so any access pattern that would require combining data from multiple items or tables at query time either has to be satisfied by data that's already been denormalized into a single item or a single partition ahead of time, or it falls back to an expensive Scan that reads broadly across the table -- there's no query-time mechanism to cheaply reconstruct relationships the way a relational join can. This is precisely why DynamoDB modeling asks you to enumerate your application's actual, specific access patterns before finalizing the table design, rather than designing a 'natural,' normalized shape first and figuring out queries later the way you might with a relational schema; the table's shape has to be built around what will actually be queried, because there's no cheap fallback if it isn't. The partition key is the single most consequential decision inside that process because it's not just about correctness -- it determines DynamoDB's underlying physical data distribution and therefore the table's actual scalability. Every item is routed to a specific physical partition based on a hash of its partition key value, and every partition has its own individual throughput ceiling; a partition key with only a few distinct values that actually appear in real traffic concentrates a large share of requests onto very few partitions no matter how much total capacity the table is provisioned with, producing the throttled-but-table-looks-healthy symptom that's the hallmark of a hot partition. A relational primary key has no equivalent physical-distribution consequence at all -- picking one column over another as the primary key doesn't determine how the database engine spreads load across its underlying storage the way a DynamoDB partition key does. So the two pieces connect directly: knowing your access patterns up front tells you which attribute or attributes need to support efficient, joinless retrieval, and picking a partition key with genuinely high cardinality relative to your real traffic -- not just any unique-sounding field -- is what turns that retrieval efficiency into actual, even scalability rather than a design that silently concentrates load onto a handful of overloaded partitions.

concepts.title: Choosing the Right AWS Data Store for the Access Pattern
concepts.description: RDS, DynamoDB, and S3 are not interchangeable options ranked by preference -- each is built around a different access pattern, and picking correctly means starting from how the data will actually be read and written, not from which service is newest or most talked about.
learningObjectives: Articulate the core access-pattern question that should drive a data store choice, before considering any specific AWS service.
Match a described workload to RDS, DynamoDB, or S3 based on its actual read/write/query requirements, not surface-level familiarity or trend.
Explain why relational flexibility (ad-hoc joins and queries) and DynamoDB's scalability are in real tension, and why you can't costlessly get both from the same store.
Identify when a single workload genuinely needs more than one data store working together, and describe a concrete example of that pattern.
Critique a data-store choice made for the wrong reason (trend-following, single-service simplicity) and propose a better-justified alternative.

sections.heading: The Question to Start From: How Will This Data Actually Be Read and Written?
sections.body:
It's tempting to choose a data store by asking 'which AWS database service should we use,' but that question skips the part that actually determines the right answer. The question worth starting from instead is: what are the specific, concrete ways this data will be queried and updated, at what volume, with what consistency requirements, and how much do those access patterns vary or stay fixed over the system's lifetime? Only after that's answered does it make sense to ask which service's underlying model matches it best -- and the honest answer is frequently 'it depends entirely on the workload,' which is a genuinely different, more useful answer than 'the newest or most-discussed service is probably the right default.'

This matters because the three data stores covered in this subject -- RDS, DynamoDB, and S3 -- aren't three competing implementations of the same underlying idea, ranked by how modern or scalable they are. They're built around fundamentally different access-pattern assumptions, and using one where the workload actually calls for another produces real, specific pain: forcing a workload that needs ad-hoc, unpredictable relational queries into DynamoDB leads straight into the expensive-Scan problem covered in the previous concept, while forcing a workload that needs massive, predictable, partition-key-addressable scale into RDS leads into the kind of instance-sizing and read-replica scaling battle that DynamoDB's model was specifically built to avoid needing in the first place.

sections.heading: RDS: When Query Flexibility and Strong Relational Guarantees Matter Most
sections.body:
RDS -- a real relational engine -- is the right default whenever the application's queries are genuinely varied and not fully known in advance, when the data has rich, meaningful relationships across entities that get queried jointly (a reporting system that regularly joins orders, customers, and products together in ad-hoc ways), or when strong transactional guarantees across multiple related writes (a multi-table `COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK` that must succeed or fail as a single unit -- moving money between two accounts is the canonical example) are a hard requirement rather than a nice-to-have. A relational engine's query planner and its indexing and join machinery are specifically built to make a wide range of query shapes reasonably efficient without redesigning the schema every time a new query need shows up, which is exactly the flexibility a DynamoDB table's access-pattern-first design deliberately trades away in exchange for its scaling properties.

The real cost of RDS shows up specifically at very high, very predictable scale: a single RDS instance has a real ceiling on write throughput (mitigated, but not eliminated, by choosing a bigger instance class or moving to Aurora's more scalable storage architecture), and horizontal read scaling requires explicitly adding and managing read replicas, as covered in the RDS concept -- there's no automatic, transparent scale-out the way DynamoDB's partition model provides. For a workload whose query needs are genuinely varied and evolving, that trade is well worth it; for a workload with a small number of fixed, extremely high-volume access patterns known well in advance, it's a cost paid for flexibility that specific workload may never actually use.

sections.heading: DynamoDB: When Access Patterns Are Known and Scale Is the Priority
sections.body:
DynamoDB is the right default when the application's access patterns are relatively small in number, well understood in advance, and need to scale to a request volume or a latency consistency that a relational engine would struggle to sustain without significant operational effort -- a high-traffic session store, a shopping cart service, an IoT device-state table receiving constant high-volume writes from millions of independent devices, or a leaderboard/counter-style workload with extremely high, predictable read/write volume against a small, well-defined set of query shapes. Its latency stays flat as the table grows, for exactly the access patterns its keys were designed around, and it scales that throughput automatically without the instance-sizing and read-replica management RDS requires.

The real cost shows up specifically when access patterns turn out to be less fixed than assumed at design time: a genuinely new query need that doesn't fit the existing partition/sort key structure or an existing secondary index either requires an expensive Scan, or requires reshaping the table (often by adding a new secondary index, or in some cases restructuring the item design entirely and backfilling). A workload that's still exploratory -- where the team doesn't yet know what questions they'll need to ask of the data -- fights against DynamoDB's core design assumption from day one, and is very often a sign that RDS's query flexibility, or a hybrid approach layering both stores, is the better starting point until the access patterns actually stabilize.

sections.heading: S3: When the Unit of Access Is a Whole Object, Not a Row or an Item
sections.body:
S3, covered in depth earlier in this subject, is neither a relational database nor a NoSQL key-value store, and it's worth being explicit about why it still belongs in this comparison: for data whose natural unit of access is a whole file or blob -- user-uploaded images and videos, PDF exports, large batch-processed data files, application logs, backups and archives -- S3 is very often the right store, not a fallback used only when a 'real' database doesn't fit. S3 has no query language at all beyond fetching by key (or listing by prefix); it is not a substitute for either RDS or DynamoDB when the actual need is to query, filter, or join structured fields within the data, but it is the clearly correct choice when the access pattern really is 'store this blob, retrieve this exact blob later by its key, at very large scale and very low per-GB cost.'

A very common, and entirely reasonable, real architecture uses more than one of these stores together for the same overall feature, each for the part of the workload it actually fits: an image-upload feature might store the actual image bytes in S3 (the object itself), a DynamoDB item for that upload's metadata and processing status keyed by upload ID (a fixed, high-volume, simple access pattern), and use RDS for the surrounding application data that genuinely benefits from relational joins and ad-hoc reporting queries -- like which users uploaded which images, tagged with which categories, queried in flexible, evolving ways by an internal admin dashboard. None of these three stores is doing the other stores' job in that architecture; each is handling exactly the part of the workload its own access-pattern strengths actually match.

sections.heading: A Framework, and a Warning Against Choosing by Trend
sections.body:
A workable decision framework asks, in order: first, is the unit of access a whole file/blob, or structured data with individual fields that need to be queried or filtered (if the former, S3 is very likely the right store for that part of the data, independent of anything else). Second, for structured data, are the access patterns few, fixed, and known well in advance, with a clear need for very high, predictable-latency scale (DynamoDB's strength) -- or are the queries varied, evolving, or dependent on joining multiple related entities together in ways that aren't fully known up front (RDS's strength)? Third, does any part of the workload have a hard requirement for multi-row/multi-item transactional atomicity across genuinely different entities (a strong signal toward RDS, or toward DynamoDB's more limited but real transaction support for a narrower set of cases)?

The warning worth stating directly: choosing a data store because it's the newest, the most discussed in industry conversation, or the one a previous project happened to use, and only afterward trying to make the actual access patterns fit it, reliably produces exactly the pain described throughout this concept -- expensive Scans bolted onto a DynamoDB table that was never designed around the query someone eventually needed, or an RDS instance straining under a workload that was always going to be simple, fixed, and enormous in volume from day one. The right sequence is the one this concept has followed throughout: understand the actual access pattern first, as concretely and specifically as possible, and let that -- not trend, not team familiarity alone, not a single service's marketing -- determine which store, or which combination of stores, actually fits.

examples.title: Same Feature, Three Data Stores Working Together
examples.code:
Feature: user-uploaded document processing pipeline

S3        -> stores the actual uploaded file bytes
             key: uploads/{userId}/{uploadId}.pdf

DynamoDB  -> tracks per-upload processing status, a fixed, high-volume,
             simple access pattern ("get this upload's current status")
             partition key: uploadId
             attributes: status, uploadedAt, s3Key

RDS       -> stores user accounts, billing plans, and admin-facing
             reporting joins ("which users on the Pro plan uploaded
             more than 10 files last month, grouped by category")
             tables: users, billing_plans, upload_metadata (foreign key to uploadId)
examples.explanation: Each store here is handling exactly the part of the workload its own strengths match, rather than one store being stretched to cover everything. S3 holds the actual file bytes because that's a pure blob-storage access pattern with no need for field-level querying. DynamoDB holds per-upload status because 'look up this one upload's status by its ID' is a fixed, extremely high-volume, single-item access pattern -- exactly DynamoDB's strength, and a poor fit for RDS if upload volume is large, since it would mean sizing and scaling a relational instance for a workload that's really just a giant key-value lookup. RDS holds the account, billing, and reporting data specifically because that admin-facing query -- filtering by plan, grouping by category, joining across users and their uploads -- is exactly the varied, evolving, join-heavy access pattern RDS is built for, and exactly the kind of query that would require either an expensive Scan or substantial redesign if it were forced into DynamoDB instead.

examples.title: The Same Access Pattern, Forced Into the Wrong Store
examples.code:
Workload: ad-hoc, evolving analytics -- "show me all orders over $500 placed
 by customers in California, grouped by product category, for any date
 range a business analyst picks in a dashboard tool"

Forced into DynamoDB:
  -> no partition key maps to "any date range, any state, any amount
     threshold, any category" -- this is a different, unpredictable
     filter combination every time an analyst uses the dashboard
  -> every such query falls back to an expensive Scan across the
     whole Orders table, reading far more data than it returns

Correctly placed in RDS:
  -> SELECT category, SUM(total) FROM orders
     JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
     WHERE customers.state = 'CA' AND orders.total > 500
       AND orders.order_date BETWEEN :start AND :end
     GROUP BY category;
  -> the query planner and appropriate indexes handle this efficiently
     without needing the exact filter combination to be known in advance
examples.explanation: This is precisely the access pattern DynamoDB's model is not built for: an ad-hoc combination of filters across multiple attributes and a related table (customers), chosen freely and differently by a human analyst each time, with no fixed, small set of known query shapes to design a partition key around. Every single distinct combination of filters an analyst might pick would need its own access pattern accounted for in the key design (or its own secondary index) to avoid a Scan, which is not realistic for genuinely open-ended, exploratory analytics. RDS handles this naturally because its query planner and indexing are built exactly for this kind of query flexibility -- the SQL query expresses the filter and join logic directly, and the database figures out an efficient execution plan without the schema needing to have been designed around this exact filter combination in advance. This is the clearest version of the RDS-vs-DynamoDB decision point from the explanation: fixed, known, high-volume access patterns favor DynamoDB; varied, evolving, join-dependent access patterns favor RDS.

examples.title: Recognizing a Trend-Driven Choice and Correcting It
examples.code:
Original reasoning: "DynamoDB is what modern, scalable teams use, so we built our
 new internal admin tool's data model on it."

Actual workload: a handful of internal staff, low request volume, and every
 week someone needs a genuinely new report -- filtered and grouped in ways
 nobody anticipated when the table was designed.

Symptom: every new report request means either a new secondary index (a
 real, recurring engineering task) or an accepted expensive Scan, for a
 workload with low overall traffic that never actually needed DynamoDB's
 scaling properties in the first place.

Corrected reasoning: low request volume + constantly evolving, unpredictable
 query needs -> RDS's query flexibility is the better fit; DynamoDB's
 scaling strength was never the actual bottleneck this workload had.
examples.explanation: The original choice wasn't wrong because DynamoDB is a bad service -- it's wrong because the justification never actually engaged with this specific workload's access patterns at all; 'modern, scalable teams use it' is a statement about the service's reputation, not about whether this particular tool's traffic volume or query variability calls for it. The symptom makes the mismatch concrete: a low-traffic internal tool was never going to stress DynamoDB's scaling advantages, but it does regularly stress the one thing DynamoDB deliberately trades away -- flexible, unanticipated query shapes -- which is exactly the cost this team is now paying repeatedly, in the form of either ongoing schema/index maintenance or accepted slow Scans. The corrected reasoning applies the framework from the explanation directly: this workload's actual profile (low volume, high query variability) points at RDS, and the fix isn't 'DynamoDB was a mistake in general,' it's 'this specific workload's access pattern was never the one DynamoDB is built to reward.'

misconceptions.description: DynamoDB is the newer, more scalable service, so it's generally the safer or more future-proof default choice for a new project's primary data store, even before considering the project's specific access patterns.
misconceptions.clarification: Scalability and query flexibility are a real trade-off, not a strict improvement running in DynamoDB's favor -- DynamoDB rewards a small number of access patterns known well in advance and penalizes ad-hoc or evolving query needs with expensive Scans or required schema/index rework, while RDS's relational query planner handles varied and unanticipated queries far more gracefully, at the cost of needing more deliberate scaling effort at very high volume. Neither profile is universally safer; the right default depends entirely on whether a given workload's access patterns are fixed and known (favoring DynamoDB) or varied and evolving (favoring RDS).

misconceptions.description: A well-architected system should pick exactly one data store and use it for everything, since using multiple different data stores for one feature adds unnecessary complexity.
misconceptions.clarification: Using more than one data store for a single feature is a normal, often correctly simpler design when different parts of that feature genuinely have different access patterns -- a blob of file bytes, a fixed high-volume status lookup, and an evolving relational reporting query are three different problems, and forcing all three into one store typically means accepting that store's weaknesses for whichever part of the workload doesn't actually match its strengths. The complexity cost of operating multiple stores is real and worth weighing, but 'one store for everything' is not automatically simpler if it means fighting a mismatched access pattern in at least one part of the system.

exercises.prompt: For each of the following three workloads, choose RDS, DynamoDB, or S3 as the primary store and justify the choice in one or two sentences based on its actual access pattern: (1) a video-streaming service's catalog of uploaded video files themselves; (2) a mobile game's leaderboard, read and written millions of times per minute by a fixed "get top 100" and "update this player's score" pair of operations; (3) a finance team's ad-hoc reporting tool where analysts write new, varied SQL-style queries against transaction data every week.
hints: For workload 1, ask what the actual unit of access is -- a whole file, or individual structured fields within it?
For workload 2, note that both operations described ("get top 100", "update this score") are fixed and known in advance, at very high volume -- which store rewards that profile specifically?

For workload 3, the defining trait is that the queries themselves change every week and aren't known in advance -- which store's query engine is built to handle that kind of variability without redesigning storage each time?
exercises.solutionCode:
workload_1: S3
  reason: "The unit of access is the whole video file itself, retrieved by key at large scale and low per-GB cost -- there's no need to query individual fields within the file."

workload_2: DynamoDB
  reason: "Both access patterns are fixed, simple, and known in advance, at very high volume -- exactly the profile DynamoDB's partition-key model scales for with flat, predictable latency regardless of leaderboard size."

workload_3: RDS
  reason: "Query needs are ad-hoc and change weekly in ways not known in advance -- exactly the varied, evolving access pattern a relational query planner and indexing are built to handle, versus DynamoDB, which would require a new access pattern (and likely a new index or Scan) for every new report shape."
exercises.solutionExplanation: Each answer follows directly from asking what the workload's actual access pattern is, rather than from any property of the service names themselves.
